plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the operation of the BUILD-MAX-HEAP procedure on a 10-element input array A = ⟨4, 1, 3, 2, 16, 9, 10, 14, 8, 7⟩ across six panels (a)–(f). At the top of the figure, the input array A is displayed as a horizontal row of ten labeled cells. Each panel shows the heap as a rooted binary tree in which every node is labeled with its array index (small numeral outside the circle) and its current key value (numeral inside the circle); light gray nodes are unmodified and the single dark gray node labeled i marks the root of the subtree currently being processed by MAX-HEAPIFY. Panel (a) shows the initial tree before any heapification, with i = 5 (value 16) — the first call to MAX-HEAPIFY starting from index ⌊n/2⌋ = 5. Panel (b) shows the state with i = 4 (value 2), after MAX-HEAPIFY has been applied at index 5. Panel (c) shows i = 3 (value 3), with the subtree at index 4 already corrected to place 14 above 2 and 8. Panel (d) shows i = 2 (value 1). Panel (e) shows i = 1 (value 4), the final call, where the root must be sifted down. Panel (f) shows the completed max-heap with root 16, in which no dark node appears and every parent holds a value greater than or equal to its children. This figure illustrates how BUILD-MAX-HEAP constructs a max-heap in place by calling MAX-HEAPIFY on each internal node from index ⌊n/2⌋ down to index 1.

demo_steps.title: Textbook six-panel view
demo_steps.narration: The default view preserves the source figure: all six heap states appear at once in a two-column by three-row layout, with the initial array A above them. The dark node labeled i marks the node about to be heapified in panels (a) through (e).

demo_steps.title: Start at the last internal node
demo_steps.narration: Panel (a) shows the initial array interpreted as a complete binary tree. BUILD-MAX-HEAP begins at i = 5, the last internal node.

demo_steps.title: Move to i = 4
demo_steps.narration: Panel (b) highlights i = 4. The previous call at i = 5 made no visible change because node 16 already satisfies the max-heap property with its child.

demo_steps.title: After heapifying i = 4
demo_steps.narration: Panel (c) shows the result of repairing the subtree rooted at index 4: 14 has moved above 2. The next highlighted node is i = 3.

demo_steps.title: After heapifying i = 3
demo_steps.narration: Panel (d) shows 10 moved above 3 in the right subtree. The algorithm now highlights i = 2.

demo_steps.title: After heapifying i = 2
demo_steps.narration: Panel (e) shows the left subtree repaired, with 16 at node 2 and 7 above 1. Now both child subtrees of the root are max-heaps, so i = 1 can be heapified.

demo_steps.title: Completed max-heap
demo_steps.narration: Panel (f) shows the final heap after heapifying the root. The largest value, 16, is at the root, and every parent is at least as large as its children.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: BUILD-MAX-HEAP works bottom-up: when a node i is heapified, its children already root valid max-heaps.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Make the default rendering a faithful static textbook layout, not an algorithm workbench: the top array spans the width above six simultaneous panels arranged as two columns by three rows. Use the exact panel states and highlights listed in the elements, including subfigure labels (a) through (f). Do not show bottom-up call-order circles, status or log text, array index labels, node index labels, comparison arrows, swap traces, or large explanatory captions in the default textbook view. Keep the optional replay control compact or collapsed so the figure dominates; selecting a replay state should only focus or lightly outline the corresponding panel while preserving the source-style visual language.

interactions.label: Implement MAX-HEAPIFY

api.does: return the array index of node i's left child
return the array index of node i's right child
return the current key stored at array index i
return true when value(i) > value(j), and record a comparison arrow between nodes i and j
exchange the values at array indices i and j; this is the only way to mutate the heap
visually mark node i with a label such as 'current' or 'largest' for the replay frame

interactions.frame: The whole array bar and matching binary tree, with the current node i shaded dark gray, comparison arrows to children, and any swap shown on both the array and tree.
interactions.success_check: After the BUILD-MAX-HEAP harness calls maxHeapify for i = floor(n/2), floor(n/2)-1, ..., 1, every parent value must be greater than or equal to both child values.
interactions.teaches: MAX-HEAPIFY repairs one subtree by repeatedly moving a too-small root downward until the local max-heap property is restored, and BUILD-MAX-HEAP works because it applies this repair from the lowest internal nodes upward.

interactions.label: Run BUILD-MAX-HEAP
interactions.teaches: The heap is not built by sorting the array; it is built by invoking the learner's MAX-HEAPIFY on internal nodes in the fixed order 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.

demo_steps.title: Start from the array-as-tree
demo_steps.narration: The array A is interpreted as a complete binary tree: children of index i are at 2i and 2i+1. Only internal nodes 1 through 5 need heapification, so BUILD-MAX-HEAP begins at i = 5.

demo_steps.title: Run the bottom-up heapify calls
demo_steps.narration: Press Run BUILD-MAX-HEAP to call your maxHeapify implementation at i = 5, 4, 3, 2, and 1. Watch each call compare a node with its children, swap with the larger child when needed, and continue downward.

demo_steps.title: Check the completed max-heap
demo_steps.narration: The final tree has 16 at the root and every parent is at least as large as its children. The array has been rearranged in place into a valid max-heap, not a fully sorted list.

plan.keyInsight: BUILD-MAX-HEAP succeeds because when MAX-HEAPIFY is called on a node, both of its child subtrees have already been made into max-heaps.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Use one large active tree rather than six static panels, but preserve the visual language of the textbook figure: pale gray circular nodes, black connecting edges, small index labels just outside the circles, large key values inside, and a dark gray current node labeled italic i. Place the array bar above the tree so swaps visibly update both representations at once. During replay, show the textbook sequence of current roots: i = 5 with value 16, i = 4 with value 2, i = 3 with value 3, i = 2 with value 1, i = 1 with value 4, then the completed heap. The final array/tree should be 16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1. Comparison arrows should be brief and directional from the current node to its children; swap highlights should connect the two nodes and the two array cells being exchanged.
